tour.title: Cyberpunk Riverfront Nights
tour.summary: One neon evening on the rivers: hotpot dinner at Jiefangbei, Hongyadong viewed free from Qiansimen Bridge, a cable-car ride across the Yangtze, and the full skyline from Nanshan hill.
tour.overviewText:
Come down to the river at six in the evening, when the fog slides off the gorges and the towers switch on floor by floor, and Chongqing stops behaving like a city and starts behaving like weather with wiring in it. This walk is your way through the famous night version — the one in all the photographs — on foot, by cable car, and with a full stomach.

Chongqing matters because geography gave it no choice. It stands where the Jialing River runs into the Yangtze, the great river the Chinese call Chang Jiang, on a peninsula of steep hills wrapped in fog for a hundred days a year. That fog hid it and fed it: some thirty-four million people live in the municipality, the direct-administered region around the city, stacked up slopes so steep that the joke writes itself. Locals call it the 8D city, meaning a place with no ground floor — and the truth inside the joke is real. Streets run across rooftops, a light-rail train passes through a block of flats, and your map's flat blue dot is lying to you about height. History doubled down. This was China's provisional wartime capital from 1937 to 1945, bombed heavily by Japan while the government held out in bunkers on these same hills. Decades later the Three Gorges Dam, raised downstream in the 2000s, drowned riverside towns across the region and moved well over a million people, many of them into this municipality — supporters call it clean power and flood control, critics mourn the drowned towns, and both facts live in the skyline you will see. Money today comes from cars, laptops and motorbikes built in the sprawling factories, plus the other industry: mala, the numbing-spicy flavour of Sichuan pepper and dried chillies that powers the city's ten thousand hotpot restaurants.

The shape of the walk is a north-to-south river crossing after dark. You start at the downtown monument square, eat hotpot early, walk down to the bridge for the free postcard view, look at Hongyadong from the outside like a local, then ride the old cableway across the Yangtze and finish above it all on the southern hill.

Early December is damp and chilly, roughly 8 to 12 degrees, with drizzle and fog that photos flatter — bring a warm layer and shoes that grip wet stone. Practicals from Hong Kong: the mainland runs on RMB, the yuan, called kuai in speech, so your Hong Kong dollars stay in your wallet — exchange some, set up mobile payment if you can, and keep cash for street stalls. Evening queues at the cableway and the hilltop run long; fees below are in yuan and worth verifying at each gate.

Eat first, photograph second, climb last. The fog is coming, and it is on your side.
tour.difficulty: Moderate. About 3.7 km of evening walking with downhill slopes, riverside steps and dense crowds, plus one cable-car ride across the Yangtze and one uphill taxi; the hilltop finish is reached by car, not on foot.
tour.bestTimeOfDay: Start around 17:30 for an early hotpot dinner, so you reach the bridge as the lights come on near 18:00. Early December nights are damp and foggy, which is exactly the look this walk wants.
tour.imageCredits: Photographs are bundled from Wikimedia Commons under public domain or Creative Commons licences. Individual credits appear under each stop's photograph.

stops.name: Jiefangbei Monument and Square
stops.entranceFeeNote: Open pedestrian square. No ticket; the crowds are the price of admission. Verify locally.
stops.openingHours: Open access daily. The square is liveliest from late afternoon past midnight.
stops.accessibility: Flat paved square, step free at street level. Evening crowds are extremely dense; wheelchair users should come before 18:00.
stops.insiderTip: Read the four faces of the column: one side honours the 1945 victory over Japan, another the 1949 liberation — the monument was renamed, not rebuilt, when power changed hands.
stops.nextStopDirections: Walk east about 160 metres, roughly 3 minutes, along the pedestrian lanes to Bayi Road. Follow the smell of chillies.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: ForwardXu, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
stops.narration:
Stand in the middle of the square and find the one old thing among the towers: a stone clock column holding the centre while glass malls lean over it. This is Jiefangbei, Liberation Monument, and it is the kilometre-zero of Chongqing.

Read it plainly. The column first went up to mark China's 1945 victory over Japan — Japan's invasion forced the government to move its wartime capital here from 1937 to 1945, and this peninsula was bombed for years while it held out. When the Communists took the city in 1949, they did not demolish the victory monument; they rededicated it to liberation and gave the square its name. One stone, two regimes, zero apologies. That is how this city edits history: by renaming, not erasing.

Now look up at the ring of towers. This peninsula, Yuzhong, the wedge between the Yangtze and the Jialing rivers, is the downtown of a municipality of some thirty-four million people — and every one of them seems to be shopping within a block of you. No ticket, no gate, just the densest acre in western China.

Walk east about 160 metres, roughly 3 minutes, following the chilli smell to Bayi Road. Dinner is the next stop, and it is not optional.

stops.name: Bayi Road Hotpot and Snack Street
stops.entranceFeeNote: Street browsing is free. A full hotpot dinner runs about ¥60–100 (yuan) per person at last check; snack stalls take cash or mobile payment. Verify prices as you order.
stops.openingHours: Stalls and restaurants daily, roughly 10:00 to 22:00, busiest at dinner. Verify locally.
stops.accessibility: Short stepped lane with wet, greasy patches and tight seating inside restaurants. Not step free; ask for a ground-floor table.
stops.insiderTip: Order a yuanyang pot — half spicy, half plain — and dip everything from the spicy side in sesame oil: the oil coat is what lets you survive the second hour.
stops.nextStopDirections: Walk north about 900 metres, roughly 12 minutes, downhill toward the Jialing River along the lanes past Xiaoshizi. The orange cable-stayed bridge ahead is Qiansimen.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Hawyih, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
stops.narration:
Stop walking and eat. The steam on your glasses is the point of this stop: you are in the hotpot capital of the world, and dinner here is fieldwork.

Hotpot, huoguo, means exactly what it says — a pot of boiling broth at the table that you cook in yourself. The Chongqing version runs on mala, the numbing-spicy flavour built from dried chillies plus Sichuan pepper, the husk that makes your lips buzz rather than burn. Legend credits Yangtze boatmen who cooked offal in chilli broth on the docks; whether or not you buy the legend, buy the economics. This is the city's edible identity, thousands of restaurants deep, and it runs all night because the fog city sweats chillies to stay warm. Order a yuanyang pot — mandarin-duck, half spicy and half plain — and mix your dip, the little bowl of sesame oil, garlic and coriander that cools each bite. A full dinner costs about ¥60–100 per person, meaning yuan, called kuai in speech, but verify as you order. Cash works; mobile payment works better.

Eat early and eat well: everything after this is walking, bridges and wind. When the buzz fades, walk north about 900 metres, roughly 12 minutes downhill toward the Jialing River. The orange cable-stayed bridge ahead is Qiansimen.

stops.name: Qiansimen Bridge Viewpoint
stops.entranceFeeNote: Public bridge walkway. No ticket. Stay on the pedestrian path and keep clear of the cycle lane.
stops.openingHours: Open access daily. Come after 18:00 when the riverside lights are on; December fog after 22:00 can swallow the view.
stops.accessibility: Step-free walkway onto the bridge, but the approach lanes are sloped and the deck vibrates as trains pass. Hold the rail in wind.
stops.insiderTip: Stand a third of the way across and look south: Hongyadong's lit cliff stacks dead centre, and the metro crossing below your feet adds the light trails for free.
stops.nextStopDirections: Walk back off the bridge to the south bank and turn east along the riverside promenade about 500 metres, roughly 8 minutes, to the front of the lit stilt-house complex.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Bill Thompson, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons
stops.narration:
Walk out onto the bridge and stop a third of the way across. Below you the Jialing runs black and fast; ahead the whole Hongyadong cliff glows gold. You have just collected the famous photograph for free — and that is the lesson of this stop.

This is the Qiansimen Bridge, the orange cable-stayed span stitching Yuzhong to the north bank, with a metro line running through its lower deck — trains you will feel through your shoes. It opened in the 2010s, part of the bridge-building spree that finally tamed a city once crossed only by ferry and cableway. And the view it sells is the one everyone wants: Hongyadong, the cliff of stacked stilt houses lit like a lantern, seen square-on across the water.

Here is the local's trick you are about to use. The crowds are all inside that glowing complex, queuing hours for the same view from between souvenir stalls. You are standing outside it, higher, centred, with the river in the frame — and it cost you nothing. Take the photo now, fog allowing, then walk back to the south bank and turn east along the promenade about 500 metres, roughly 8 minutes, to see the cliff up close.

stops.name: Hongyadong Riverside Promenade
stops.entranceFeeNote: The promenade is free. Entering the complex is also unticketed but involves long queues and timed crowd control on weekend evenings. Verify locally.
stops.openingHours: Promenade open access daily. The complex lights run roughly 18:00 to 23:00; verify locally.
stops.accessibility: The promenade is level but packed shoulder-to-shoulder after 19:00. The complex itself is eleven steep floors with lifts overwhelmed by crowds — view from outside.
stops.insiderTip: Count the floors from the river: eleven storeys, with the top floor meeting the clifftop street — the building is the staircase the hill always needed.
stops.nextStopDirections: Walk east along the riverside road about 1.5 km, roughly 25 minutes, past Chaotianmen toward the cableway's north station on Xinhua Road. The towers follow the cliff the whole way.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Youyiy33, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
stops.narration:
Now you are standing at the foot of the lantern. Look up: eleven storeys of wooden balconies and glowing eaves climb the cliff, with the towers of the peninsula stacked behind like chaperones.

What you are looking at is diaojiaolou, stilt houses — the wooden homes on stilts that once clung to every cliff and riverbank in this region, built out over the drop because flat land was too precious to waste. The old Hongyadong was that: poor, crowded, half falling into the Jialing. This version, rebuilt in the 2000s, is the idea of it turned into a vertical street of restaurants and souvenir shops. Supporters call it heritage rescued; critics call it a theme park wearing an old neighbourhood's clothes. Both have a point, and the lights at 18:00 settle the argument for most visitors.

So here is the honest advice: do not go in. Not tonight. The interior is eleven steep floors of queuing between identical stalls, and everything worth seeing — the cliff stack, the stilts, the glow — is visible from exactly where you stand, free. When you have stared enough, walk east along the riverside road about 1.5 km, roughly 25 minutes, toward the cableway's north station on Xinhua Road.

stops.name: Yangtze River Cableway
stops.entranceFeeNote: Ticketed ride: about ¥20–30 (yuan) one way at last check. Evening queues can exceed an hour; the cabins run through the night lights. Verify price and hours at the gate.
stops.openingHours: Runs daily, roughly 07:30 to 22:30. Verify locally; boarding can close early when queues cap out.
stops.accessibility: Steps and steep ramps at the north station; cabins fit wheelchairs with staff help but boarding is timed and brisk. Evening queues involve long standing.
stops.insiderTip: Ride southbound after dark and stand at the front of the cabin: the car swings out over black water and Yuzhong's skyline rises to meet you like a lit wall.
stops.nextStopDirections: This is a cable-car ride, not a walk: the south bank is about 1.2 km across the water, five minutes by cabin against an impossible swim, so ride it. From the south station walk about 600 metres, roughly 10 minutes, east along the river to Longmenhao Old Street.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: rheins, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
stops.narration:
Buy the ticket and get in the little box. You are about to cross the Yangtze the way Chongqing did it before the bridges — through the air.

The cableway, suodao, opened in 1987, when this city of millions had almost no river crossings and commuters queued daily to dangle over the water to work. The car you are riding is their bus: about 1.2 km of cable, five minutes over black water, from the Xinhua Road station here in Yuzhong to the south bank. A one-way ticket costs about ¥20–30, yuan, but verify at the gate — and budget the queue, not the ride, because evening lines can exceed an hour. Ride southbound after dark and stand at the front: the cabin swings off the cliff and the whole peninsula rises ahead of you, every floor lit, fog chewing the tops.

The mechanism worth pocketing: this was infrastructure first and attraction second, demoted by bridges into a monument that still works. Commuters abandoned it; the night turned it into theatre.

From the south station, walk about 600 metres, roughly 10 minutes east along the river to Longmenhao Old Street. The view back is the next stop.

stops.name: Longmenhao Old Street
stops.entranceFeeNote: Open historic street. No ticket; teahouses and bars price in yuan. Verify menu prices as you order.
stops.openingHours: Open access daily. The street is at its best from dusk to about 23:00 when the skyline across the water is lit.
stops.accessibility: Old stone lanes with steps, slopes and uneven slabs. Not step free; the smoothest ground is the riverside terrace at the street's north edge.
stops.insiderTip: Take your nightcap on the riverside terrace, not inside: the Yuzhong skyline across the water is the entertainment, and it is free.
stops.nextStopDirections: This is a taxi hop, not a walk: the hilltop is about 4 km up winding roads, over eighty minutes on foot uphill in the dark, so do not walk it. Take a taxi or ride-hail 10 to 15 minutes up Nanshan to the Yikeshu viewing platform. Agree the fare or check the app price first.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: 麦丝鱿鱼, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
stops.narration:
Step off the cableway's hurry and slow down. The stone lanes in front of you are Longmenhao, the old south-bank waterfront — warehouses, inns and foreign firms from the treaty-port century, rebuilt into teahouses and bars that face the best free show in Chongqing.

Turn around. Across the Yangtze, the whole Yuzhong peninsula stands lit: the towers you walked under at dinner, the bridge you crossed, the Hongyadong glow, all of it doubled in the water. This is the reverse shot of your evening — the postcard's answer — and the locals on the terrace beside you are watching it instead of any screen. That is the lesson: Chongqing's cyberpunk look is not a filter. It is a mountain city that builds upward because it cannot build outward, seen from the dark bank it left behind.

Browsing is free; tea and drinks price in yuan, so verify menus. One note for planners: Ciqikou, the old porcelain-town lanes west of the centre, is a separate evening entirely — save it for another night. When the skyline has done its work, do not walk to the last stop. The hilltop is about 4 km up winding roads, over eighty minutes on foot uphill in the dark. Take a taxi 10 to 15 minutes up Nanshan to the Yikeshu platform.

stops.name: Nanshan Yikeshu Viewing Platform
stops.entranceFeeNote: Ticketed viewing platform: about ¥30 (yuan) at last check. Verify prices at the gate; fog can close or flatten the view with no refund of the climb.
stops.openingHours: Open daily, roughly 09:00 to 22:30. Verify locally; come before 22:00 for the full lit panorama.
stops.accessibility: Viewing terraces reached by ramps and steps from the drop-off; guard rails throughout but the ground is steep and can be slick in drizzle. Not step free.
stops.insiderTip: If the fog has eaten the far bank, photograph the near bridges instead: the light trails on the interchange below are sharper in mist than any skyline.
stops.nextStopDirections: End of the walk. Ride-hail or taxi back down to the Nan'an riverfront and the metro; the hill road is dark, so agree the fare in the app before you descend. In December the wind up here bites — zip up before the car comes.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: 杨志强Zhiqiang, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
stops.narration:
Get out of the car, climb the last steps, and turn around. Below you the two rivers meet around the lit peninsula, bridges strung with light trails, fog taking bites out of the towers. This is Yikeshu — One Tree — the viewing platform on Nanshan, the southern hill, and the whole evening lying flat under you like a circuit board.

Read it from up here, because height finally explains the joke. The 8D city is not a slogan: streets stack on rooftops, the rail runs through a building, and districts pile vertically where flat cities sprawl. Fog made it defensible in war, rivers made it rich in trade, the dam's resettlements filled its towers, and the chillies keep it awake. Entry costs about ¥30, yuan, verify at the gate — and if the fog has eaten the far bank, photograph the interchange below instead. Mist sharpens light trails.

End of the walk. You ate fire at street level, crossed the Jialing on a bridge, skipped the Hongyadong queue like a local, dangled over the Yangtze in a 1980s cabin, and finished above it all. Ride-hail back down to the Nan'an riverfront and the metro, and zip up — December bites hardest at exactly this height.
